storylines.latest_title: Loom: Shared memory, document search, and code indexing for AI agents

prior_narrative.tldr: In early September a startup and an academic paper both proposed giving AI agents persistent, shared memory instead of siloed per-session context. The pitch: context one agent learns should stay usable by every other agent on the same team, not vanish when a session ends.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Motif open-sourced a shared, versioned memory store for teams of coding agents on Sept 21, following MemHub's commercial persistent-memory product and a kernel-managed-memory research paper earlier in the month.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: If cross-agent shared memory catches on, plan for memory-consistency and access-control problems, not just context loss — evaluate write conflicts before adopting a shared store.

beats.headline: MemHub ships persistent shared memory for coding agents
arXiv paper proposes kernel-managed shared memory for multi-agent personalization
Motif open-sources shared memory for teams of coding agents

open_questions: Does Motif or MemHub define a conflict-resolution model for concurrent agent writes to shared memory?
Does kernel-managed shared memory, the arXiv proposal, ship in any production agent framework, or does it remain research?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before adopting a shared-memory layer for a multi-agent team, test how it handles concurrent writes and stale reads — none of September's three releases publish a consistency model.

prior_narrative.tldr: On Oct 31 DeepSeek's harness team put the architecture of dsh-superagent, an always-on router-worker coding agent, on GitHub as a research prototype. Press coverage from Nov 1 to Nov 4 framed it as a challenge to Claude Code that watches team chat for work and fixes bugs on its own.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Former DeepSeek core member Zhang Bo open-sourced a separate personal agent on Nov 20 that reportedly runs a 125B model locally on a 12GB GPU; it is not a DeepSeek release.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: dsh-superagent is a published reference design for a proactive, chat-triggered coding agent from a frontier lab, but it ships as a research prototype and every capability claim so far comes from press rewrites, not hands-on evaluation.

What license does dsh-superagent ship under, and which models can its router and workers use?
Will DeepSeek move dsh-superagent beyond a research prototype into a maintained product?
Does the 125B-on-12GB claim for Zhang Bo's agent hold up, and at what quantization and speed?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Read the dsh-superagent repo as a design reference for chat-triggered agents, but do not deploy it until a license and an independent evaluation exist.

storylines.latest_title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models

prior_narrative.tldr: This thread is a reading list of LLM research grouped by shared wording, not one event. From Oct 30 it ran through pruning, Anthropic's Nov 2 provable-inference update, knowledge editing and eval-validity work to Nov 13-16 papers on when a model should abstain, ask or escalate.
prior_narrative.whats_new: Nov 18: a contrastive-prototype method detects jailbreak prompts without training a separate guard model, after Nov 16-17 papers on calibrated abstention thresholds and provenance-aware decoding for omnimodal hallucinations.
prior_narrative.why_it_matters: Most items are single unreplicated preprints, but the recent run converges on guardrail design: calibrated refusal, modality-aware hallucination control and lightweight jailbreak screening, each a component a serving stack can test.

beats.headline: Efficiency work: extreme-sparsity pruning and an early-stopping audit for reasoning models
beats.summary: Opens the window; a text-to-SQL architecture survey lands the same day.

beats.headline: Anthropic reports progress on zkSNARK-based provable inference
beats.summary: The thread's only lab-published item: cryptographic proofs applied to LLM inference.

beats.headline: Updating what models know: answerability drift, multimodal unlearning and lifelong knowledge editing
beats.summary: Also here: an LLM choosing federated aggregation rules without training.

beats.headline: Judgment under scrutiny: rising rater standards on Chatbot Arena, framing effects and personality benchmarks
beats.summary: These days also bring an LLM AutoML searcher, physics-guided fault diagnosis, a training-simulation benchmark and a cognitive account of learning by thinking.

beats.headline: What do scores measure? ShadowBench and a corrupted-input study probe shortcuts behind passing evals
beats.summary: One tests recall without explicit entity names; the other asks whether LLMs pass NLI on noun-stripped or shuffled inputs.

beats.headline: Knowing when not to answer: black-box uncertainty and an interactive ambiguity-resolution eval
beats.summary: One splits prompt ambiguity from knowledge gaps via API calls only; the other scores when a model should ask versus assume. A tabular anomaly-detection paper lands the same day.

beats.headline: Applied decisions: budgeted malware triage, annotation benchmarking, agent RL environments and an AI-infrastructure survey
beats.summary: The run moves from model internals to LLMs making operational calls under cost and documentation constraints.

beats.headline: Guardrails at the output: calibrated abstention, provenance-aware decoding and jailbreak detection
beats.summary: Nov 16-18 papers each target a control point between the model and the user: when to refuse, which modality to trust, which prompt to block.

open_questions: Does the contrastive-prototype jailbreak detector report false-positive rates on benign prompts and hold up against adaptive attacks?
Does stability-compensated threshold calibration keep its error guarantee when the deployed model or prompt distribution shifts?
Does PACD report the decoding latency or extra forward passes it adds per token?
Does TRIAGE-CPG report which models escalate too rarely or too often under a fixed analysis budget?
Do published unlearning or knowledge-editing methods still pass when probed without explicit entity names, as ShadowBench suggests they may not?
Does Anthropic publish proving cost or latency figures for zkSNARK-based provable inference?
prior_narrative.take_for_builders: Before swapping in any of these guardrails, replay your own traffic: measure the jailbreak detector's false-block rate on benign prompts, check that a calibrated abstention threshold holds its error rate on your data, and count the extra model calls each method adds.
